title: Organisational structure
overview: Organisational structure determines reporting relationships, authority, communication and decision speed. You must compare functional, hierarchical/flat/narrow and matrix structures, understand grouping by product/function/geography, and analyse delegation, accountability, span of control, centralisation/decentralisation and line/staff relationships.
syllabusPoints: Link organisational structure to business objectives.
Compare functional, hierarchical and matrix structures and grouping by function/product/geography.
Explain structural change, growth and delayering.
Use hierarchy, chain of command, span of control, responsibility, authority, delegation and accountability.
Explain how structure can support growth, flexibility and intrapreneurship.
Analyse the relationship between span of control, hierarchy, control and trust.
Distinguish structures organised by product, function and geographical area.

definitions.definition: The number of subordinates directly managed by one manager.
The route through which authority/instructions pass through an organisation.
Passing authority for a task/decision to a subordinate while ultimate accountability remains with the manager.
Decision authority concentrated at senior/head-office level.
Decision authority distributed to lower levels, divisions or locations.
Removing one or more management levels from the hierarchy.
The formal right to make decisions, give instructions and use organisational resources.
The duty to complete an assigned task or achieve an agreed result.
A role with direct authority for activities that contribute to the organisation's main objectives.
A specialist advisory or support role without direct authority over the line manager's operations.

sections.title: Tall/narrow and flat structures
content: Tall structures have more levels and often narrower spans: close supervision and clear promotion routes but slower communication and higher management cost. Flat structures reduce layers and often widen spans: faster communication and more delegation but heavier manager workloads.

Growth may initially add specialist departments and hierarchy, but later delayering can remove duplicated supervision. The useful test is not whether the chart looks flat: it is whether decisions, information and accountability reach the people who can improve the objective.
bullets: A wide span can reduce management cost and give employees autonomy, but one manager may have too little time to coach or control many inexperienced subordinates.
A long chain of command can filter or delay information, so customer problems reach decision-makers slowly and service or sales may suffer.
Delayering removes levels, not work: remaining managers need training, information and authority or workloads and decision errors may rise.

examples.label: Delayering a retail chain
examples.content: Removing regional supervisors may save salaries and let store managers change staffing quickly. If each area manager now oversees 30 stores, however, weaker coaching and control may increase stock loss and inconsistent service.

sections.title: Functional structure
content: A functional structure groups specialists such as marketing, finance and operations. It supports expertise, career development and economies of specialisation but can create silos and slow cross-functional coordination.

A product structure groups responsibility around product lines, while a geographical structure groups it around regions or countries. These divisional structures increase focus and local accountability but duplicate functions and can encourage rivalry or inconsistent decisions.
bullets: Product divisions can measure each range's revenue and profit and respond quickly to its customers, but separate marketing or finance teams increase cost.
Geographical divisions can adapt to local laws and cultures, but head office may lose control and global customers may receive inconsistent service.
Functional grouping best exploits scarce specialists when products and locations share similar needs.

sections.title: Matrix structure
content: Employees report across two dimensions such as function and project/product. It improves cross-functional collaboration and resource sharing, but dual authority can create conflict and unclear priorities.

A matrix can support innovation and intrapreneurship because engineers, marketers and finance staff solve a project problem together. It needs agreed priorities, conflict-resolution rules and transparent resource allocation so employees do not receive incompatible instructions.
bullets: Projects gain several specialist perspectives without permanently duplicating each specialist in every division.
Frequent meetings and negotiation can slow decisions and raise coordination cost.
Performance appraisal is harder when functional and project managers disagree about an employee's priorities.

sections.title: Delegation and accountability
content: Delegation develops employees and frees managers for higher-level work. It succeeds when objectives, authority, resources and competence are clear. The subordinate becomes responsible for the task and answerable for performance, while the manager remains ultimately accountable for the decision to delegate and the final result.
Accountability requires agreed standards, reporting and review. Too much control signals distrust and slows local action; too little control can produce inconsistent or risky decisions.
bullets: Delegation without enough authority creates responsibility without the power to deliver.
Trust can increase initiative and speed, but should be supported by competence, information, limits and proportionate monitoring.
Successful delegation can enrich jobs, prepare future managers and release senior time for strategy.

sections.title: Centralisation versus decentralisation
content: Centralisation supports consistency, strategic control and standardisation. Decentralisation can improve local responsiveness, motivation and decision speed. The right balance depends on size, risk, staff skill, geographic spread and need for common standards.

A business may centralise brand, finance and safety rules while decentralising prices, staffing or product choices. This selective approach protects high-risk decisions without making every local response wait for head office.
bullets: Decentralisation uses local knowledge and can motivate managers through real authority, improving response to customers and competitors.
It may duplicate expertise, weaken purchasing economies and produce incompatible decisions across divisions.
Centralisation is more persuasive where decisions create legal, financial or reputation risks across the whole organisation.

sections.title: Line and staff relationships
content: Line managers have direct authority for core operational results; staff specialists advise or support with expertise. Conflict can occur if line managers see advice as interference or staff specialists lack operational context.

The distinction concerns authority, not seniority. A legal specialist may be highly paid yet advise an operations manager who remains responsible for the decision and its workforce and business-performance consequences.
bullets: Staff experts can improve decisions where regulation or technology is complex.
Advice can delay action or be ignored unless roles, escalation rights and final decision authority are clear.
Line managers should supply operational evidence; staff specialists should explain risks and workable alternatives.

comparisonTable.title: Structure trade-offs
rows: Slow communication and higher management cost
Clear market focus and local accountability
Duplicated functions and weaker central control

diagram.title: Structure-performance chain
nodes: Cost, quality, speed and growth outcomes

analysisChains.title: Delayering
steps: Remaining managers gain wider spans of control
analysisChains.evaluation: Savings and speed must be weighed against heavier workloads, weaker supervision and possible loss of experienced staff.

analysisChains.title: Decentralising a multinational
steps: Regional managers gain authority over local products and prices
Decisions use closer knowledge of customers and competitors
Response time falls and the offer better fits local demand
Sales and market share may rise
analysisChains.evaluation: Benefits depend on capable managers and controls; duplication or inconsistent branding can raise cost and damage global reputation.

analysisChains.title: Matrix team for a new product
steps: Specialists from several functions share information
Technical, customer and financial problems are identified earlier
Rework and launch delay may fall
The product reaches market faster and revenue starts sooner
analysisChains.evaluation: Dual reporting can create conflict and meeting cost; clear project authority and priorities are required.

examTips: Link structure to size, geography, rate of change, workforce skill and objectives.
When discussing delayering, analyse both lower cost/faster communication and workload/promotion drawbacks.
Delegation transfers authority, not all final accountability.
Compare structures against the same objective: speed, control, innovation, cost or local responsiveness.
commonMistakes: Confusing span of control with number of hierarchy levels.
Assuming every flat structure is decentralised.
Ignoring dual reporting conflict in matrix structures.
Treating line/staff as junior/senior employee categories.

quickRecall.question: What is a span of control?
quickRecall.answer: The number of subordinates who report directly to one manager.

quickRecall.question: How does delayering change structure?
quickRecall.answer: It removes management levels, usually shortening the chain of command and widening remaining spans of control.

quickRecall.question: What is delegated and what is retained?
quickRecall.answer: Authority for a task is delegated; the manager normally retains ultimate accountability for the result.

quickRecall.question: Why can a matrix structure create conflict?
quickRecall.answer: Employees may answer to functional and project managers who set different priorities.

quickRecall.question: When is geographical grouping useful?
quickRecall.answer: When regions differ in customer needs, culture, law or competition enough to require local decisions.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between line and staff functions?
quickRecall.answer: Line managers have direct authority for core results; staff specialists advise or support them.
